why: What each `include:` family delivers, as source column names. Greek and Hebrew are different
languages and their analyses differ, so a family is edition-shaped: it emits whichever of its
columns the edition actually has, and nothing merges the two ontologies. A Greek verb has
tense, voice and mood; a Hebrew verb has stem and state. A Greek sense is a Louw-Nida number;
a Hebrew sense is an SDBH domain. Declaring both sets under one family lets the same code
serve both editions without knowing anything about either language.
Container field names are the source's column names, verbatim. Nothing here is a name we
invented, so any field a consumer receives can be traced back to a column.
`morph` is deliberately absent from `morphology`. Both editions carry it as a packed string
duplicating the decomposed columns beside it, and shipping the same information twice costs

ids.purpose: The word's source identifier, so annotation can be joined back to the text.

morphology.purpose: Grammatical analysis per word, in whatever categories the edition analyses.

senses.purpose: Lexical semantic domain per word, in the edition's own sense system.

glosses.purpose: Word-level glosses, for a reader or a prompt rather than for analysis.

referents.purpose: Participant reference, the strongest cohesion signal above the clause.

discourse.purpose: Discourse features and notes, resolved against the text being read.

syntax.purpose: The constituency tree, standoff: a list with one entry per sentence. Requires `ids`.

notes.lang: Hebrew only, and not strictly morphology — it distinguishes Hebrew from Aramaic, which selects a different paradigm, so it travels with the analysis that depends on it.
notes.usx_attributes: `lemma` and `strong` are attributes USX already defines on a `char` element with marker `w`, so they go there rather than into the container. The list gives the source columns that fill each, in order of preference: Greek names its Strong's column `strong`, Hebrew names it `strongnumberx`. These two are the only renames anywhere in this file, and they exist because the destination is spec-defined.
notes.not_carried: `morph` (packed duplicate), `normalized` and `transliteration` (alternative forms of `text`), `greek` and `greekstrong` (Hebrew-to-Greek alignment, not a property of the Hebrew word), `stronglemma` (a lemma spelling of the Strong's entry), `mandarin` is carried under `glosses` alongside `english`.
notes.frame: Carried under `referents`. It was listed as not carried, on the grounds that a syntactic frame belongs with `syntax` — filed before `include: [syntax]` was ruled standoff. The `syntax` payload is the constituency tree with leaves carrying only references, so a per-word attribute cannot ride in it: in Lowfat terms `syntax` is the `wg` tree and `frame` is an `m` leaf attribute. Families are organised by form, and `frame` is the semantic-role counterpart to `subjref`'s grammatical one — they come apart at a passive whose subject is the undergoer, where `subjref` reads no change and `A0` against `A1` states one. Present in both corpora.
